newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries open lower before housing, jobless.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries open lower before housing, jobless.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices opened moderately lower on Thursday before the release of government data on January housing starts and weekly jobless claims.
The benchmark 6-1/2 percent 30-year bond opened at 100-13/32, down 6/32, to yield 6.59 percent.

Government traders will analyze three economic reports today, all of which typically attract some market attention. The first two -- January housing starts and new jobless claims for the week ended February 15 -- are released simultaneously at 0830 EST/1330 GMT.
Economists polled by Reuters forecast, on average, that housing starts rose to an annualized 1.42 million in January from an annualized 1.329 million in December.
Jobless claims rose to 323,000 in the latest week from 309,000 a week earlier, the economists also estimated.
Participants linked the market's early weakness, however, to other factors, including weakness in the global bond market.
"Overnight you had some important German economic data," said Josh Stiles, senior bond strategist at I.D.E.A. An index of the German business climate gave a strong reading, he said.

A surprise boost in Germany's M3 money supply boosted the market but also weighed on European bond prices, he said. Japanese bonds also weakened as Japan announced a plan to help deal with problem real estate loans at Japanese banks.
Meanwhile, the focus of the U.S. market is changing, Stiles said.

"The market is coming into this period where the focus shifts from low-inflation news to upcoming supply and Humphrey-Hawkins," said Stiles, referring to next week's two- and five-year Treasury note auctions and to Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's Feb 26 Senate testimony.
With those significant events on the calendar, "hedge funds led the way in starting to book some profits," Stiles said.
Participants said the market is expecting a bounce in housing starts.

Regarding jobless claims, "nobody really believes initial jobless claims are as low as the 309,000 that printed last week," said Stiles. "But claims below 350,000 are still consistent with monthly payroll growth of 200,000 jobs, so that's not necessarily bullish for bonds," he said.

The market also gets the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia's index at 1000 EST/1500 GMT. The February index is expected to read +10.0, off a bit from +11.3 in Janaury. Before the housing data came out, three- six- and year-bill rates were each up one basis point to 4.97 percent, 5.04 percent and 5.18 percent, respectively.
Two-year notes were down 1/32 to 100-3/32, yielding 5.82 percent. Five-year notes were down 3/32 at 100-16/32, yielding 6.13 percent. Ten-year notes were down 4/32 at 99-13/32, yielding 6.33 percent.
